cues.text: An angle in radians is the length of its circular arc divided by the radius.
A full turn is two pi radians, so one hundred eighty degrees equals pi
radians.
Multiply degrees by pi over one hundred eighty to convert them.
One hundred fifty degrees is five pi over six.
On the unit circle, the point at angle theta has horizontal coordinate cosine
theta and vertical coordinate sine theta.
Tangent is sine divided by cosine when cosine is nonzero.
Secant is the reciprocal of cosine, cosecant the reciprocal of sine, and
cotangent is cosine divided by sine where defined.
The coordinates give quadrant signs without a separate memorized sign rule.
At two pi over three, the reference angle is pi over three, but the point is
in
quadrant two.
Its cosine is negative one half and its sine is square root of three over two.
Useful reference values are sine pi over six equal to one half, sine pi over
four equal to square root of two over two, and sine pi over three equal to
square root of three over two.
Cosine reverses that list by complementary angles.
Use exact fractions and radicals until a numerical approximation is requested.
A graph helps separate a function's domain from its range.
Sine and cosine accept every real angle and produce values from negative one
to
one inclusive.
They repeat after two pi.
Sine is odd, so sine of negative x is negative sine x; cosine is even, so
cosine of negative x equals cosine x.
Tangent repeats after pi and has every real number as an output, but it is
undefined at pi over two plus an integer multiple of pi.
Its graph has vertical asymptotes there.
Cotangent also has period pi and all real outputs, with excluded inputs at
integer multiples of pi.
Secant shares cosine's excluded zeros and has period two pi.
Cosecant shares sine's excluded zeros and also has period two pi.
Their outputs have magnitude at least one, so neither can equal zero.
For a scaled function sine of two x, the least positive period is pi.
A nonzero vertical scale changes amplitude without changing that period.
A horizontal shift moves the graph while preserving its basic range and
period.
State excluded input values whenever a denominator vanishes.
An asymptote is a boundary of a graph branch, not an extra point where an
infinite real output is assigned.
The unit circle has equation horizontal coordinate squared plus vertical
coordinate squared equals one.
Substituting cosine and sine gives sine squared x plus cosine squared x equal
to one.
Divide this identity by cosine squared x where cosine is nonzero to obtain one
plus tangent squared x equal to secant squared x.
Dividing by sine squared x instead gives one plus cotangent squared x equal to
cosecant squared x.
These identities retain the restrictions created by division.
For example, one minus cosine squared x divided by sine x simplifies to sine x
only when sine x is nonzero in the original expression.
The simplified formula is defined at additional inputs, but those points do
not
automatically belong to the original expression.
If sine x equals three fifths, cosine squared x equals sixteen twenty fifths.
Cosine may be plus or minus four fifths; its sign needs a quadrant condition.
If x is in quadrant two, cosine is negative four fifths.
Squaring can determine a magnitude while losing sign information.
To prove an identity, work on a common domain and transform one side using
valid steps.
A few numerical checks may disprove an incorrect identity, but they do not
prove it for every permitted input.
Compound angle identities connect an angle sum or difference to familiar
values.
Sine of A plus B equals sine A cosine B plus cosine A sine B.
For a difference, change the middle sign to minus.
Cosine of A plus B equals cosine A cosine B minus sine A sine B; the
difference
formula uses plus instead.
Keep this opposite sign pattern visible.
To find sine fifteen degrees, write fifteen as forty five minus thirty.
Substitution gives square root of six minus square root of two, all divided by
four.
Tangent of A plus B is the sum of tangent A and tangent B divided by one minus
their product, where the component tangents and the final denominator are
defined.
For tangent fifteen degrees, use the difference formula with forty five and
thirty.
The result simplifies to two minus square root of three.
If a component tangent is undefined, the sine and cosine sum formulas may
still
evaluate the angle, so a tangent formula is not a universal replacement at
every input.
Compound identities can be derived from unit circle rotations and then checked
at zero.
They do not say that sine of a sum is the sum of the two sines.
Set both angles equal in the compound identities.
This gives sine two x equal to twice sine x cosine x, and cosine two x equal
to cosine squared x minus sine squared x.
Replacing one square using the fundamental identity gives one minus twice sine
squared x or twice cosine squared x minus one.
Repeated use of the compound formulas gives sine three x equal to three sine x
minus four sine cubed x, and cosine three x equal to four cosine cubed x minus
three cosine x.
Half angle formulas follow by rearranging the double angle identities.
Sine squared of x over two is one minus cosine x divided by two, and cosine
squared of x over two is one plus cosine x divided by two.
Taking square roots requires the sign from the quadrant of the half angle.
If x equals four pi over three, its half is two pi over three, so the half
angle cosine is negative one half, not positive one half.
Tangent of x over two can be written as sine x divided by one plus cosine x
where that denominator is nonzero.
A rearranged formula may have a different exceptional set, so keep the
conditions of the form actually used.
Compound angle formulas can be added or subtracted to transform sums into
products.
Set u as half the sum of A and B and v as half their difference.
Then A equals u plus v and B equals u minus v.
Adding their sine expansions gives sine A plus sine B equal to twice sine of
their half sum times cosine of their half difference.
Their cosine sum similarly becomes twice cosine of the half sum times cosine
of
the half difference.
For products, twice sine A cosine B equals sine of A plus B plus sine of A
minus B.
Twice sine A sine B equals cosine of A minus B minus cosine of A plus B.
Signs matter because changing the order of a sine difference reverses it.
As an exact value example, sine seventy five degrees plus sine fifteen degrees
becomes twice sine forty five degrees times cosine thirty degrees, giving
square root of six divided by two.
These forms are also useful for equations: a product equals zero when at least
one of its factors is zero.
Before dividing out a factor, consider whether it can vanish and supply a
separate solution family.
A trigonometric equation generally has periodic families of solutions.
Sine x equals sine alpha when x is alpha plus an integer multiple of two pi,
or
pi minus alpha plus an integer multiple of two pi.
Cosine x equals cosine alpha when x is plus or minus alpha plus an integer
multiple of two pi.
Tangent x equals tangent alpha when x is alpha plus an integer multiple of pi,
provided the values are defined.
Now solve sine two x equals sine x on the interval from zero inclusive to two
pi exclusive.
The double angle identity gives sine x times two cosine x minus one equal to
zero.
Keep both factors.
Sine x equal to zero supplies zero and pi in this interval.
Cosine x equal to one half supplies pi over three and five pi over three.
There are four distinct solutions.
Dividing by sine x at the start would lose zero and pi.
Sort the final list and remove duplicates that arise when periodic families
coincide.
If a transformation involved squaring or a denominator, substitute the
candidates into the original equation.
Interval endpoints must be checked according to whether they are included,
rather than copied from a memorized cycle.
A linear combination of sine and cosine can be written as one shifted sine.
Let R equal the square root of a squared plus b squared.
If R is positive, choose an angle phi whose cosine is a over R and whose sine
is b over R.
Expanding R sine of x plus phi gives a sine x plus b cosine x.
The quadrant of phi must match both ratios, not just a tangent quotient.
Since sine ranges from negative one to one over all real inputs, the
combination has range negative R to R, with both extremes attained.
For three sine x plus four cosine x, R equals five, so its maximum is five and
minimum negative five.
An independent bound follows by applying the vector dot product inequality to
the coefficient vector and the unit circle vector.
If both coefficients are zero, the expression is constantly zero and no phase
angle is needed.
A restricted input interval may prevent one of the extreme values from being
attained, so the unrestricted range cannot always be copied to an interval
problem.
Distinguish this amplitude calculation from adding the separate maxima of sine
and cosine, which may occur at different inputs.
Sine, cosine and tangent repeat their values, so each needs an appropriate
restriction before an inverse function is defined.
We use arcsine with outputs from negative pi over two to pi over two,
including
both endpoints.
Arccosine returns an angle from zero to pi inclusive.
Arctangent returns an angle strictly between negative pi over two and pi over
two.
Arcsine and arccosine accept real inputs only from negative one to one, while
arctangent accepts every real input.
The notation sine inverse means arcsine here, not the reciprocal cosecant.
Sine of arcsine x equals x throughout the inverse domain.
Reversing the composition needs care: arcsine of sine theta equals theta only
when theta is already in the principal sine interval.
For theta equal to five pi over six, sine theta is one half, so arcsine
returns
pi over six instead.
Arctangent of tangent three pi over four returns negative pi over four, the
principal angle with tangent negative one.
Arccosine of cosine negative pi over three returns positive pi over three.
Find the function value first, then select the unique angle in the declared
principal range.
The remaining inverse functions also need explicit principal branches.
In this class, arccotangent accepts every real number and returns an angle
strictly between zero and pi.
Arcsecant accepts inputs with absolute value at least one and returns an angle
from zero to pi, excluding pi over two.
Arccosecant has the same input restriction and returns an angle from negative
pi over two to pi over two, excluding zero.
Both endpoints of that latter interval remain included.
Some references choose different conventions, so retain these declarations
when
applying identities.
For arccotangent of negative one, the required angle lies in quadrant two and
equals three pi over four.
For arcsecant of negative two, solve cosine theta equal to negative one half
in
the arcsecant range, giving two pi over three.
For arccosecant of negative two, solve sine theta equal to negative one half
in
its chosen range, giving negative pi over six.
Secant and cosecant cannot have magnitudes below one, which explains their
inverse domains.
Check a proposed answer by applying the original function and checking the
principal range.
A correct ratio at an angle outside that range is not the chosen inverse
value.
Inverse identities come from both function values and branch restrictions.
For x between negative one and one inclusive, arcsine x plus arccosine x
equals
pi over two.
If theta is arcsine x, its complement pi over two minus theta lies in the
arccosine range and has cosine x.
This proves the identity across the whole domain.
Under our arccotangent convention, arctangent x plus arccotangent x also
equals
pi over two for every real x.
The complement of an arctangent output lies strictly between zero and pi.
Arcsine is odd, so arcsine of negative x equals negative arcsine x.
Arccosine instead satisfies arccosine of negative x equal to pi minus
arccosine
x.
For input magnitude at least one, arcsecant x equals arccosine of one over x,
and arccosecant x equals arcsine of one over x under the stated branches.
As an equation example, set arcsine x equal to twice arccosine x.
Combining it with the complementary sum gives arccosine x equal to pi over six
and x equal to square root of three over two.
Substitute back and check that x belongs to both inverse domains.
The tangent addition formula does not by itself determine the value of an
inverse tangent sum.
Let A be arctangent u and B be arctangent v.
When one minus u v is nonzero, tangent of A plus B is u plus v divided by
one minus u v.
Applying the principal arctangent to that quotient may shift the actual sum by
pi.
For u equal to one half and v equal to one third, both angles are positive and
their sum is less than pi over two.
The quotient equals one, so the sum is pi over four.
For u equal to two and v equal to three, both angles lie between pi over four
and pi over two.
Their sum is between pi over two and pi.
The tangent quotient is negative one, so the sum is three pi over four, not
negative pi over four.
If u and v are both one, the sum is pi over two; the zero denominator warns
that the tangent quotient is undefined there.
Use the original angles to handle that case.
In every inverse identity calculation, retain the real input domains and
determine the output interval before choosing the final angle.
